verses.note: The promise of kings points ahead to Israel's monarchy, to David, and through him to the Messiah. It is repeated to Jacob (35:11) and focused on Judah (49:10).

Esau's family has an organized government of chiefs within a generation or two, while Jacob's sons are still herdsmen without land. Genesis records the contrast without resentment: the power the world sees first is not the kingdom God is building.

Israel's kingship is promised before it exists and arrives late. The Bible's hope for a king is shaped from this early point by waiting on God's timing rather than by imitating the nations (compare 1 Samuel 8:5).

Kingship in Israel is first promised in a family blessing, long before Israel has a king. The rule of God's people is set within God's promise from the start, not invented later as a political convenience.
The king exists for the people's sake. God's purpose in establishing David is that Israel, ‘my people’, may live securely in the place he appoints.
Chronicles' wording draws out what Samuel implies: the throne of David is the throne of the LORD's kingdom (compare 1 Chronicles 29:23). Israel's king rules on God's behalf.
God's kingdom is exercised through the king he appoints and from the place he chooses. The New Testament's Zion is the heavenly Jerusalem where the Son reigns (Hebrews 12:22-24).

The psalm closes the lament of one sufferer with the universal reign of God. The pairing of the suffering one and the coming kingdom anticipates the Gospels' proclamation of a kingdom that comes through the cross.

The king's power is measured by what it serves. Humility (anvah) is an unexpected virtue in a war song, and it anticipates the Messiah of Zechariah 9:9 who comes to Zion righteous and humble, and Revelation 19:11, where the rider on the white horse judges and wages war in righteousness.

The throne lasts forever, echoing God's promise to David (2 Samuel 7:13-16), and its scepter is mishor, level uprightness, a word used for level ground and for fair judgment (Isaiah 11:4). An everlasting reign is good news only if it is a just one.

The verse describes a reign that is already real while opposition remains. The New Testament's pattern of the kingdom already inaugurated and not yet complete (Christ reigns now, and the last enemy, death, is yet to be destroyed, 1 Corinthians 15:25-26) is built on exactly this picture.

God's reign ends oppression first and war second. The burning of boots and bloodied cloaks anticipates Isaiah's picture of swords beaten into plowshares (2:4) and Psalm 46:9's God who burns the chariots. The kingdom Isaiah hopes for is not a better-armed Judah but a world where the equipment of war has no further use.

The reign on David's throne is defined by justice and righteousness, the very qualities Israel's kings failed to deliver (5:7). God's kingdom is not simply God's power but God's right order established on earth, and verse 7 makes it everlasting and ever growing.

The king's rule is only as good as his character, and the verse makes righteousness and faithfulness the things that hold him together. Isaiah's kingdom is never merely a transfer of power to Israel; it is the reign of a king whose own integrity makes justice possible for everyone under him.

The good news is that God reigns. Isaiah's herald brings not advice or a program but an announcement of a new state of affairs. Jesus began preaching in Galilee with the same news, that the kingdom of God had come near (Mark 1:14-15), and the New Testament's word for gospel comes from this herald's verb.

The permanence promised to David's line in 2 Samuel 7:16 is here renewed after the monarchy had collapsed. The Old Testament's hope for God's kingdom is tied to a ruler of David's line who reigns forever, the hope announced to Mary in Luke 1:32-33.

The kingdom of God in Daniel is not an abstraction; it is given to a person and shared with a people. Jesus' announcement that the kingdom of God has come near (Mark 1:15) and his claim that all authority in heaven and on earth had been given to him (Matthew 28:18) stand on this verse.

The kingdom is received, not seized. The saints do not overthrow the beasts; the court removes the beasts and the kingdom is given. Jesus' promise that the Father is pleased to give the little flock the kingdom (Luke 12:32) has the same shape.

The same everlasting kingdom is given to the son of man (verse 14) and to the people of the saints (verse 27). The New Testament holds the two together: the kingdom belongs to Christ and is shared with those who belong to him (Luke 22:29-30; Revelation 3:21).

The ruler's shepherding produces security for his people and extends to the ends of the earth. The kingdom joins care for a particular flock with universal reach, the pattern of Psalm 2:8 and Psalm 72:8.
The oracle ends by setting the ruler's peace of verses 4-5 against judgment on the disobedient. God's kingdom brings security to those who listen and justice against those who do not.
The king's rule is universal, but it spreads by proclamation of peace, not by chariots. Zechariah pictures a kingdom that removes the tools of war first from God's own people.

God's rule ends in a flourishing people on a fruitful land. The chapter's movement from judgment to a humble king to a festive harvest shows that the kingdom's goal is abundant life, not conquest for its own sake.
The verse introduces Matthew's central theme. God's reign is not a place above the clouds but God acting as king, and John announces it as near enough to demand a decision now.

What the devil offers from a high mountain, the Father gives on a mountain in Galilee after the cross: “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to Me” (28:18). The kingdom Jesus will announce in verse 17 is not taken by bargain but received from God.

The first thing Jesus proclaims is not himself but God's reign drawing near. The perfect tense holds together what the rest of Matthew holds together: the kingdom is already pressing into the present in Jesus' words and works, and still to come in fullness.

The kingdom comes as word and deed together. Jesus announces God's reign and then shows its presence by undoing sickness, which is why his answer to John the Baptist points to both (11:4-5) and why the disciples receive authority to do the same (10:1, 10:7-8).

The kingdom is given, not achieved, and it is given first to those who come with nothing. The beatitude reverses the world's judgment of who is fortunate by making dependence on God, not strength, the mark of the kingdom's people.
The repeated promise ‘theirs is the kingdom of heaven’ brackets all eight beatitudes, so every quality between them describes the kingdom's people.

To pray ‘Your kingdom come’ is to ask for God's reign, already present in Jesus, to arrive in its fullness. The petition keeps disciples looking forward to the day when earth fully obeys, as heaven does now.
The kingdom is not only prayed for (verse 10) but actively sought. Seeking it first puts every other good in its place without despising it.
Entering the kingdom of heaven is tied to doing the Father's will, the very will disciples pray to see done on earth in 6:10.

The verse pictures the kingdom's future as a feast already set, with the patriarchs as hosts. It joins the kingdom Jesus announces to the promise made to Abraham that all the families of the earth would be blessed through him (Genesis 12:3).

In Luke's version the command continues, “You, however, go and proclaim the kingdom of God” (Luke 9:60). The urgency comes from the kingdom's arrival: the time of decision has come, and those who do not answer are, in the saying's hard language, dead.

The ‘gospel of the kingdom’ is the announcement that God's reign has arrived in Jesus, and the healings are its evidence. By repeating 4:23 Matthew makes chapters 5 to 9 one portrait of the kingdom's coming, in word and in deed.

The announcement and the works belong together. The disciples do not only say that God's reign is near; they show it in bodies healed and people freed, which is how the kingdom's nearness becomes visible before its fullness.

The kingdom's peace does not arrive by avoiding conflict. Because Jesus' claim is total, it separates those who receive him from those who refuse him, and the verse warns that loyalty to him will cost some disciples the peace of their homes before it brings the peace of God's reign. The sword is the division his claim causes, not a weapon his followers wield (26:52).

The verse marks a turn in the ages. John stood at the threshold of the kingdom and pointed to it; the least disciple stands inside it and sees what John announced. Greatness in the kingdom is a matter of where God's history has placed a person, not of personal merit.

On any reading, the kingdom's arrival provokes a response of force. If hostile, the verse explains John's prison and anticipates Jesus' death: God's reign advances through suffering. If favorable, it describes the urgency of those who press in. Either way, the kingdom is not a quiet idea but a power that divides.

The saying assumes two opposed kingdoms, Satan's and God's. Jesus' exorcisms are not a quarrel inside the realm of evil but an assault on it from outside, which sets up the claim of verse 28 that God's kingdom has arrived.

This is one of the clearest statements that the kingdom is already present in Jesus' ministry. It stands beside sayings that it is near (4:17) and still to come (6:10), and together they describe a reign that has arrived in part and awaits its fullness.
The kingdom comes as an invasion of occupied territory. Satan is strong, but Jesus is stronger, and every person freed from demonic power is plunder taken back for God.

The parable is a word about the kingdom's outcome before it is a word about hearers. In spite of path, rock, and thorns, the harvest comes. Jesus has already called the crowds a harvest waiting for workers (9:37-38), and the image of harvest belongs to the end of the age (verse 39). The disciples, discouraged by the rejection of chapters 11 and 12, are told that the sowing is not failing.

The verse marks the turn of the ages. What the prophets saw from a distance, the disciples see in Jesus, which means the kingdom is not only future; its arrival is visible now in his words and deeds (11:4-6, 12:28). Peter later says the prophets searched for the time of the Messiah's sufferings and glories (1 Peter 1:10-12).

The parable describes the kingdom in the present as a field where good seed and bad grow together. God's reign has begun, but it has not yet removed evil from the world, and the parable warns against expecting it to look pure before the harvest.

The kingdom that seemed so small in Jesus' Galilean ministry will grow to a size no one could predict from its seed. The contrast between beginning and end, not a slow evolution, is the parable's point.

The kingdom works from within and out of sight, until everything is changed. Jesus uses the same image for the Pharisees' teaching as a corrupting influence (16:6, 11-12), and Paul for sin in the church (1 Corinthians 5:6-8), which shows that the image carries no fixed moral value; here it pictures the hidden power of God's reign.

The Son of Man's kingdom (verse 41) and the Father's kingdom (verse 43) are one reign seen at two moments: the present rule of the risen Son, in which good and evil are mixed, and its completion when the Son hands the kingdom to the Father (1 Corinthians 15:24-28).

The kingdom is worth more than everything else a person has, and the one who sees that gives up everything with joy, not grief. The man finds the treasure unexpectedly, which fits the gift language of verse 11: the kingdom is found, not manufactured.
The kingdom of God is his reign breaking into history in Jesus. The healings and exorcisms in the rest of the chapter show what that reign looks like when it arrives.
The demon asks whether Jesus has come to destroy them, and the answer implied by the story is yes. The arrival of God's kingdom means the end of the powers that hold people captive.
The authority of Jesus' teaching is shown by the authority of his action. In Mark the kingdom is not only announced but demonstrated.
The argument assumes that Satan has a kingdom, an organized dominion, and that Jesus' exorcisms are invading it. The kingdom of God announced in 1:15 comes as a conflict of kingdoms.

What has been given is the secret that God's reign has arrived in a form no one expected: in a Galilean teacher and a handful of followers, hidden as seed is hidden. The parables that follow all describe that hiddenness.

The kingdom grows by God's power, not by human anxiety or technique. The sower's part is to sow and to wait; the growth is given. Paul says the same of his own ministry: one plants, another waters, God gives the growth (1 Corinthians 3:6-7).

The kingdom's end is out of all proportion to its beginning. The parable asked Jesus' first hearers to believe that a teacher with a few disciples in Galilee was the beginning of God's reign over the nations.

The kingdom's power frees what was bound. Jesus' command to silence belongs to the pattern scholars since William Wrede (The Messianic Secret, 1901) have discussed: he will not have his identity proclaimed through wonders apart from the cross. Yet the kingdom cannot be kept quiet, and the news spreads in spite of him.

The call to the cross follows directly on Jesus' own. The disciple's road is shaped by the master's: the kingdom is entered by those who give up the claim to rule their own lives, and the cross they carry is theirs, not a metaphor for ordinary hardship.

The verse promises a visible arrival of the kingdom's power within the lifetime of some who heard it. The chapter note sets out the readings: the transfiguration, the resurrection and Pentecost, the fall of the temple in AD 70, or the final coming. Mark's placement makes the transfiguration at least a first fulfillment; John Chrysostom, among the fathers, read it that way (Homilies on Matthew 56), and 2 Peter 1:16-18 speaks of the mountain as the eyewitness sight of Christ's power and coming.

The kingdom reverses the ordinary ladder of rank. Jesus does not forbid the desire to be first; he redirects it into service of all, which in 10:43-45 he grounds in his own coming not to be served but to serve.

The kingdom belongs to those who, like little children, have no status to bring and no claim to press. The verse turns the disciples' sense of who deserves Jesus' time upside down, as the whole chapter will turn the order of first and last (verse 31).
The scribe has understood the law's center but has not yet entered. The kingdom is entered by following the one who says this, not only by agreeing with his summary of the law.

Even on the night of betrayal Jesus speaks with certainty of ‘that day’ in the kingdom of God. The Lord's Supper therefore carries a forward look, which Paul states as proclaiming the Lord's death ‘until he comes’ (1 Corinthians 11:26).

Jesus neither refuses the title nor explains it. John's longer account makes the point explicit, that his kingdom is not from this world (John 18:36); Mark lets the rest of the chapter show what kind of king he is, crowned with thorns and enthroned on a cross.

Joseph is ‘waiting for the kingdom of God’ at the moment the King lies dead. His hope, and his courage in acting on it, show that faith can act before it understands, which is exactly what Easter will reward.
‘His kingdom will never end’ gives the reign of David's heir the permanence Daniel 7:14 gives the kingdom of the Son of Man, joining the two strands of hope in one person.

The devil's claim to hand out kingdoms is left unrefuted in the moment but overturned by the Gospel: authority over all things is given to the Son by the Father (10:22; Daniel 7:14), and the kingdom comes through suffering (24:26).
The unclean spirits obey a word. The kingdom Jesus proclaims arrives as a liberation of people held captive by evil, the release of verse 18 made visible (compare 11:20).
The kingdom of God is the content of the good news, and it is announced before it is explained. Luke uses the phrase some thirty times, beginning here.
The restored hand is a small instance of the restoration the prophets promised. The kingdom comes as healing, and the Sabbath, the day of rest, becomes the day of restoration.
The kingdom belongs now to the poor. Luke's first beatitude fulfills Jesus' program to ‘preach good news to the poor’ (4:18) and reverses the world's order before explaining it.

The saying marks a turn of the ages. John stands at the threshold as the greatest of the prophets, and the kingdom Jesus brings is greater than all that led to it. Luke 16:16 states the same division: the Law and the Prophets until John, and since then the good news of the kingdom.

Luke defines Jesus' travels by their message: he goes everywhere announcing God's reign as good news. The kingdom is not first a program but a proclamation, and the deeds in the rest of the chapter show what the proclaimed reign does.
The kingdom has ‘mysteries’: God's reign is arriving in a form that can be missed, like seed in soil, and it is recognized only by those to whom its meaning is opened.
The kingdom is proclaimed and shown together. Healing is not an advertisement for the message but part of its content: where God reigns, demons and diseases give way.
Jesus meets the crowd's intrusion with welcome, teaching, and healing, and then with food. Luke presents the kingdom as hospitality that goes further than anyone asked.

The hungry are filled, as the beatitude promised, and there is more than enough. Isaiah pictured the LORD preparing a feast for all peoples on his mountain (Isaiah 25:6), and Jesus speaks of people coming from east and west to recline in the kingdom (13:29). The feeding is a foretaste of that table.

Interpreters have referred the promise to the transfiguration that follows, to the resurrection and Pentecost, to the fall of Jerusalem in AD 70, or to the spread of the church in Acts. Many ancient readers, John Chrysostom among them, took it of the transfiguration, a reading Luke's placement supports. Luke's wording, ‘see the kingdom’, suits a present glimpse of the kingdom's reality rather than its final arrival.

The kingdom's claim outranks even the most sacred family duty. The saying is not a general rule against burial or honoring parents (18:20), but a demand that when Jesus calls, the call comes first, because the proclamation of life has an urgency that nothing else has.

Fitness for the kingdom is described not as ability but as undivided attention. The three conversations have no endings, which leaves the reader in the would-be followers' place, asked to decide what comes first.

The kingdom of God is announced as having drawn near to a town through the presence of Jesus' messengers and the healing of its sick. God's reign is not an abstraction but arrives in bodies made well and in a message that calls for response.

The exorcisms by Jesus' messengers are signs that Satan's power is being broken. God's reign advances at the expense of the kingdom of evil, a conflict Luke develops in 11:20-22 and brings to its climax in the cross and resurrection.
To pray for the kingdom to come is to confess that it has not yet fully come. Yet in verse 20 Jesus says it has already come upon his hearers, so the prayer asks God to complete what he has begun.
Jesus speaks of Satan as having a kingdom, an ordered realm of power over people. The coming of God's kingdom is therefore not only the gathering of a people but the overthrow of a rival reign.

God's reign has arrived wherever Jesus frees people from evil by God's power. The kingdom is present in his works, not only promised for the future, though the disciples still pray for its coming (verse 2).

The kingdom comes as a rescue from occupation. Jesus' exorcisms are raids on a strong man's house, and the plunder distributed is people set free, a victory completed, as Colossians 2:15 says, at the cross.

The kingdom's arrival forces a decision. Luke also records the opposite-sounding saying, ‘whoever is not against you is for you’ (9:50), about an exorcist working in Jesus' name; together they say that allegiance to Jesus, not membership in a particular group, is the dividing line.

The kingdom is the object of the disciples' seeking, not an add-on to ordinary life. Those who seek God's reign are given what they need along the way, as Solomon, who asked for wisdom rather than riches, was given riches as well (1 Kings 3:11-13).

The kingdom is the Father's gift, not the disciples' achievement. Jesus later confers it on the apostles as the Father conferred it on him (22:29), fulfilling the vision in which the kingdom is given to the holy people of the Most High (Daniel 7:27).

Shame for opponents and joy for the people are how Luke marks the kingdom's arrival: what Jesus does divides the audience. The crowd's joy anticipates the multitude of disciples praising God for all the mighty works as Jesus nears Jerusalem (19:37).

Placed after the healing of one woman in one synagogue, the parable says that such small beginnings are the kingdom's real presence, not a preface to it. The birds' nesting points ahead to the gathering of the nations described in verse 29.

The kingdom works from within and out of sight until its effect is total. Leaven was often an image of corruption (12:1, 1 Corinthians 5:6), so the parable is surprising, but Jesus says plainly that the kingdom of God is like it: the image here is of pervasive power, not of impurity.

The kingdom's reversals run through Luke from Mary's song (1:52-53) onward. The saying warns against assuming a place and holds out hope to those who have none, without turning the reversal into a rule that every insider is lost.
The kingdom's order of honor is set by God, who, as Mary sang, brings down rulers and lifts up the humble (1:52). Seeking a high place before God is the surest way to lose it.

The kingdom's future is pictured as a meal, and the guest is right that those who eat it are blessed. The parable that follows moves the blessing from a future assumption to a present decision: the invitation is being issued now.

The banquet is ready before anyone arrives, and the guests are asked only to come. The verse pictures God's kingdom as a gift prepared in full, with the invitation as the only point where human beings enter the story.
The kingdom is not only a future hope here but a present proclamation that people are entering. The verse marks John as the point where promise becomes announcement.
The kingdom is not the kind of thing that arrives on a timetable readable by observation. The verse turns the question from ‘when’ to ‘where’ and ‘who’, which verse 21 answers.

On either translation the verse teaches that God's reign is present now, before any cosmic sign. ‘Among you’ locates it in the person and works of Jesus (11:20); ‘within you’ stresses that it is received and ruled in the heart. Many readers hold the two together, but neither allows the kingdom to be reduced to human potential without the king.

The kingdom belongs to the helpless and dependent. The verse has been cited on both sides of the infant baptism debate (Calvin, Institutes 4.16.7, for it; Tertullian, On Baptism 18, counseling delay), and believer-baptist traditions reply that it speaks of blessing, not baptism. Its plain teaching is that no one is too small or too empty-handed to be welcome.

Luke does not deny that the kingdom is near (10:9, 21:31) or already present in Jesus (17:21). He denies that it would appear at once in the form the crowd imagined, a public restoration triggered by Jesus' arrival in Jerusalem. The disciples ask the same question after the resurrection (Acts 1:6), and they receive the same kind of answer.

The kingdom in this parable is resisted before it is fully revealed. Luke does not present rejection of Jesus as a surprise to God's plan but as part of what the king foresaw, and the refrain ‘we do not want this man’ anticipates the choice of Barabbas over Jesus (23:18-25).

Luke names the kingdom of God as what is near, keeping the whole discourse within his central theme. The kingdom already present in Jesus (17:21) moves toward its public fullness, and the signs mark its approach as surely as leaves mark summer.

The Passover looked back to the exodus; Jesus says it also looks forward, to a fulfillment in the kingdom of God. Luke has already pictured that kingdom as a feast where people come from east and west to recline (13:29, 14:15), the banquet Isaiah foresaw (Isaiah 25:6-8).

The kingdom is given as a covenant gift, from the Father to the Son and from the Son to his followers. It is not seized, as the Gentile kings seize power (verse 25), but received, and it is shared at a table.

The inscription is the chapter's one public proclamation of Jesus' kingship, posted by the Roman state as a joke. Luke leaves it standing over the cross because it is true: the kingdom of God comes through a king who will not save himself.

The criminal is the one person at the cross who speaks of Jesus' kingdom without mockery. He believes the kingdom is real while its King is dying, which is the paradox of the whole chapter: the kingdom of God comes through the cross, not around it.

Joseph was waiting for the kingdom of God, and the kingdom's King lies dead. His act of burial is the faith of a man who still expects God's reign though he does not yet know how it will come; the reader knows that the next chapter will answer him.
John's one use of the Synoptic phrase ties Jesus' preaching of the kingdom to the new birth: the kingdom is entered by people whom God has remade, not by descent or merit.

Jesus is a king, as John will make plain at his trial and on the cross (18:37, 19:19), but not one made by a crowd's force. He tells Pilate that his kingdom is not from this world (18:36). The feeding shows the king's power; the withdrawal shows the kind of kingship he refuses.

Jesus accepts the title King of Israel but defines his kingship by the donkey rather than the war horse. The kingdom he brings comes in humility and peace, and its throne, John will show, is the cross (19:19).

The verse contrasts sources, not locations. Christ's reign does not arise from the world's power and does not defend itself by the world's weapons, which is why his servants do not fight. It is nonetheless present in the world, standing before Pilate and claiming him.

Israel's Scriptures confess the LORD as Israel's king (Judges 8:23, 1 Samuel 8:7, Psalm 47:7). The chief priests' cry is a denial of that confession for the sake of a political settlement. John does not say it of the Jewish people as a whole; he says it of the leaders at this moment, and the choice it exposes, a lesser king preferred to God, is one every reader can make.

Pilate means the title as a warning to would-be rebels; John presents it as a proclamation in the languages of the known world. The kingship of Jesus is announced publicly, over the cross, to everyone who passes by.
Those who receive grace will reign in life. Humanity's lost vocation to rule (Genesis 1:28) is restored in Christ, and the redeemed share his reign (2 Timothy 2:12, Revelation 5:10).

Christ reigns now, and his reign is aimed at an end: every opposing power abolished and the kingdom handed to the Father. The kingdom has a present and a future, and verse 24 describes the future's completion.
The kingdom's final shape is God all in all. Christ's reign is not a rival kingdom to the Father's but the means by which the Father's rule is restored to the whole creation.

The kingdom of God in its fullness is something inherited, received as a gift, and it requires a new kind of existence that mortal nature cannot supply. The kingdom's coming involves the remaking of the people who enter it.

The final bowing of every knee is the completion of God's rule over creation. It is future in form (every tongue should confess), and Christian traditions differ over whether it describes the joyful worship of the redeemed only or also the forced acknowledgment of those who resisted.
The kingdom is described as the kingdom of the Son, a present reality into which believers have already been moved. It is not only a future hope but a change of rule that has already happened.
The ‘until’ of the psalm frames the present age: Christ already reigns, and his reign will be complete when every enemy is subjected, the last being death (1 Corinthians 15:25-26).
The powers of the age to come are already at work in the church. The verse shows the overlap of the ages: the future world is tasted now, in the word and in works of power, before it arrives in full.

Christ reigns now and waits for the full subjection of his enemies. The verse places the church in that interval: the decisive work is done, the final victory is certain and still to come (1 Corinthians 15:25).

Amillennial and postmillennial readers connect this binding with Jesus' saying about binding the strong man (Mark 3:27) and with his casting out of the ruler of this world at the cross (John 12:31): Satan is restrained now so that he cannot keep the nations from hearing the gospel. Premillennial readers note that the New Testament still describes Satan as actively deceiving (2 Corinthians 4:4; 1 Peter 5:8) and expect a fuller binding after Christ's return.
